extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, logic, and natural philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and standards for defining and identifying causes, laws of nature, and related concepts (e.g., permanence, capacity, conservation of force) in philosophical and scientific reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause as unconditionally invariable antecedent
rubrics_metrics.description: The cause of a phenomenon is 'the antecedent, or the concurrence of antecedents, on which it is invariably and unconditionally consequent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unconditionalness (necessity) is essential: we must believe not merely that the antecedent has always been followed by the consequent in past experience, but that, given the present constitution of things, it always will be so. The example of day and night shows that mere invariable succession in past experience is insufficient if the succession is conditional on some other antecedent (e.g., the sun rising).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invariable sequence is not sufficient for causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Invariable sequence, therefore, is not synonymous with causation, unless the sequence, besides being invariable, is unconditional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequences that are uniform in past experience may nevertheless be only accidental conjunctions or conditional sequences (e.g., day and night, earth's orbital motions). We should distinguish unconditional sequences (causal) from conditional sequences that depend on other antecedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate conditions of a phenomenon must be among immediately preceding facts (but prior causes can produce capacities)
rubrics_metrics.description: The conditions required for a phenomenon—the antecedents required for calling it into existence—must all be found among the facts immediately, not remotely, preceding its commencement; yet earlier causes may produce capacities or states in objects that function as conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: painting a wall confers a lasting property (a 'state of preparation') enabling future sensations of whiteness; gunpowder collocation produces readiness to explode. Such capacities are not substantive present facts unless they consist in a physical collocation of particles; otherwise they are names for our assurance that an object will act in a particular way under new circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between positive assemblage-of-conditions and inclusion of negatives
rubrics_metrics.description: If one confines the word 'cause' to the assemblage of positive conditions without the negative, then instead of 'unconditionally' one must say 'subject to no other than negative conditions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a convenient modification of the cause-definition: define the cause as the set of positive antecedent conditions which, provided no counteracting (negative) conditions exist, will be followed by the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuance of cause vs. continuance of effect (instantaneous vs sustained phenomena)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some effects, once produced, continue without the continued presence of the cause; others require the permanent presence of the agencies which produced them at first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many things persist until changed (plowshare, corpse) although their causes have ceased. Some phenomena (illumination, mercury in a tube) are instantaneous facts that perish and must be perpetually reproduced while conditions subsist. Thus, in analysing causation, distinguish whether continuance of a cause is necessary to maintain an effect or merely to reproduce it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cause and effect may be contemporaneous; precedence resolves direction
rubrics_metrics.description: A cause does not necessarily stand in time anterior to its effect by any appreciable interval; the effect may commence simultaneously with its cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When two co-existent phenomena are in doubt as to which is cause and which effect, determine which preceded the other if possible. Whether cause and effect coincide in time or one follows the other does not alter the practical relation that the beginning of a phenomenon implies a cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: One phenomenon may produce heterogeneous effects (properties/powers language)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the same phenomenon is followed by effects of different and dissimilar orders, it is usual to say that each different sort of effect is produced by a different property of the cause (e.g., gravitative and magnetic properties of the earth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terms like 'properties' and 'powers' are convenient abstract names denoting connections between different effects and the object producing them; they are instruments of abridgment and conceptual economy but explain nothing beyond the observed connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent (primeval) causes and limits of inferable laws
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist permanent causes (primeval natural agents) whose origin we cannot account for; the distribution of these primeval causes is not itself reducible to a law, and from their local distribution we cannot infer their distribution elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the distribution of primeval causes appears irregular and lawless, co-existences among effects that depend on such primeval causes are not genuine laws of nature but contingent on the local co-existence of agents. Treat primeval causes as ultimate facts for which no earlier causes are discoverable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-existences of effects are derivative, not independent laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Co-existences among effects cannot be original and independent laws distinct from laws of causation; uniformities of co-existence are results of identity or co-existence of their causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Except when different properties of the same cause produce different effects, co-existences of effects from different causes will not be universal laws. Only co-existences between different properties of the same natural agent can claim the character of independent laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation of Force — empirical equivalence of forms of force
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical facts show that agencies formerly regarded as distinct sources of force (heat, electricity, chemical action, nervous action, momentum) are interchangeable in definite and fixed quantities with one another: the amount of one can be quantitatively equated with another (e.g., a quantity of heat corresponding to 772 foot-pounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This part of the doctrine rests on experimental and observed equivalences: when one form of force disappears another appears in equivalent quantity, and reversing the process recovers the same quantity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservation of Force as hypothesis (reduction to motion and potentiality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The higher-stage hypothesis of the doctrine asserts that Conservation of Force is Conservation of Motion, requiring molecular motions and, by some accounts, a pervading ether; more defensibly, 'force' should be conceived as 'potentiality of motion' rather than actual motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reduction to motion involves hypothetical entities (molecular motions, ether) and is not strictly proven; it is useful but must be treated as hypothesis. Recognize 'potential energy' (stored capability to produce motion) and that not all manifestations require actual continuous motion.

rubrics_metrics.name: In assembling the cause distinguish force and collocation
rubrics_metrics.description: In specifying the assemblage of conditions that constitutes a cause, distinguish two elements: (1) the presence of a force (a changing antecedent) and (2) the collocation or position of objects required for the particular transmutation which constitutes the phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any production of change requires both collocations (stationary antecedents) and at least one changing antecedent (a force). Examples: a bonfire requires fuel, air, spark (collocations) and chemical action (force); a mill requires collocation of parts and the moving force of water or wind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation involves an element of belief beyond mere observation
rubrics_metrics.description: To call something a cause requires belief that the antecedent will always be followed by the consequent so long as the present constitution of things endures; this belief is not derived from mere past succession but from experience that teaches which uniformities are conditional and which are unconditional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish belief grounded in further experiential knowledge (e.g., experiments with the sun) from mere observed sequence. The notion of necessity in causation amounts to unconditionalness under the current constitution of nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical value of retaining the term 'cause' and treating events as causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Rejecting the term 'cause' (as M. Comté and some others suggest) risks losing a convenient generalization; designating events as causes is a useful abstraction that need not commit one to a dubious metaphysical theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use 'cause' as a practical general name for antecedent phenomena which reliably produce consequents; abandoning the term forfeits a fundamental distinction useful for framing a Canon of Induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deterministic implication: current state and laws determine future states in principle
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of the whole universe at any instant is believed to be the consequence of its state at the previous instant such that one knowing all agents, collocations, and laws could, in principle, predict the whole subsequent history of the universe (barring intervention by a controlling volition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This presents a philosophic/deterministic implication of causal laws: theoretical predictability is in principle possible though practically infeasible due to complexity; acknowledges limits if volition intervenes.
